situation:
You are the people operations lead at NORTHGATE WATCH SECURITY, a two-year-old company that provides uniformed guards and access monitoring for office buildings. The founder (judge), who also serves as chief executive, has asked you to recommend how the company should fill twenty guard positions that a new building contract requires within ninety days.

The company has about seven months of its first round of funding left. When it started, it published a hiring commitment: openings would be posted internally first, and the guard force would be built to reflect the neighborhoods it protects. The commitment is written into the work rules the guards signed and into the contract with the company's largest client.

A referral channel could fill all twenty posts in three weeks at no agency cost. It draws from one former employer's alumni network, and the company's applicant tracking system shows that channel has produced nearly the same profile every time: licensed, experienced, and almost entirely from outside the neighborhoods the commitment names. Using it means the postings the guards were promised never appear.

Open recruiting through community partners and the tracking system would honor both halves of the commitment, but licensing new applicants takes eight to ten weeks and the outreach costs money the company would take out of the runway it has left. Missing the ninety-day date carries a penalty in the building contract, and the longest-serving guards have been waiting on a supervisor posting since spring.

The founder (judge) wants your recommendation on how the twenty positions get filled, and on what the company says to the guards who were promised those postings. You will present your recommendation to the founder (judge) in the founder's office. The founder (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the questions, the founder (judge) will thank you for your work.
